claims.text: The initial Co-free FeNiCrMn single crystal is a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The initial material is free of precipitates and grain boundaries.
Yield onset is governed by thermally activated dislocation nucleation.
Dislocation glide is hindered by severe lattice friction in FeNiCrMn.
The severe lattice friction is caused by chemical short-range order.
Chemical disorder among the constituent elements impedes dislocation glide.
There is no sufficient driving force for tensile-stress-induced FCC-to-BCC transformation in equiatomic FeNiCrMn.
FCC-to-BCC transformation is kinetically suppressed at strain rates associated with high dislocation accumulation.
Dislocation nucleation occurs at point defects or surface steps.
Lattice-friction-dominated plasticity causes yield strength to depend only weakly on strain rate.
Thermal activation over the lattice-friction barrier is less strain-rate-sensitive than dislocation multiplication in pure metals.
The stacking-fault energy and lattice stability of FeNiCrMn disfavor FCC-to-BCC transformation relative to slip.
No detectable FCC-to-BCC transformation will occur during yielding, including at high strain rates.
Crystal orientation will significantly affect yield strength through anisotropic slip-system activation.
Slip rather than transformation will remain the operative mechanism for both [111] and [100] orientations.
Traditional FCC metals such as pure Ni and Cu have strongly strain-rate-dependent yield strength because of dislocation multiplication and drag.
Above 600 K, diffusion-controlled creep may dominate and permit different transformation pathways.
Significant deviations from equiatomic composition may alter stacking-fault energy and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
The cited CoNiCrFeMn nanowire simulations exhibit twinning and FCC-to-HCP transformation rather than identifying BCC transformation as a deformation mode.
Fe, Ni, Cr, and Mn constitute five principal elements.

contradictions.description: The alloy is consistently named Co-free FeNiCrMn, which contains four listed elements, but the structural mediator calls Fe, Ni, Cr, and Mn 'five principal elements.'

Transformation suppression is attributed both to kinetic suppression at high strain rate and to an absence of thermodynamic driving force, without distinguishing or reconciling these two explanations.
